```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# knitr weaves each guide in its own session; the width is restored at the end
# anyway, as the CRAN Cookbook asks for every option that is changed.
.opciones_previas <- options(width = 90)
# Without DBI, RSQLite and duckdb (all suggested) the chunks that query the
# databases do not run and the guide is still built; the inline figures then
# say "varios".
tiene_motores <- requireNamespace("DBI", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("RSQLite", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("duckdb", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = tiene_motores)
cifra <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x) || !length(x) || is.na(x)) return("varios")
  format(x, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
}
porcentaje <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x) || !length(x) || is.na(x)) return("varios")
  paste0(cifra(round(100 * x, 1)), " %")
}
n_padron <- n_visitas <- n_cubiertas <- n_huerfanas <- NA
cobertura_cruda <- cobertura <- NA_real_
```

> This guide is the English version of
> [12. Cruzar dos bases](cruzar-dos-bases.html). `lupa` writes its messages
> and tables in Spanish, so the output below is in Spanish.

A registry lives in one SQLite database. The visits live in a DuckDB database.
The credential that opens one does not open the other, and no query can name
both at once. How do you know whether every visit finds its person? And how do
you turn that question into a measure that can be repeated for every delivery?

> **In this guide:**
>
> - profiling each table in its engine with `perfilar_dbi()`;
> - reading only the keys, in blocks, with `DBI::dbSendQuery()` and
>   `DBI::dbFetch()`;
> - comparing the coverage in R with `detectar_relaciones()`;
> - turning the comparison into a metric with `medir()` and
>   `ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad`;
> - deciding what to do when the keys do not have the same type or the same
>   shape.

## Two databases, one question {#dos-bases-una-pregunta}

The example has 8 people in the registry and 20 visits. The visits store the
person as a 2-digit text with a leading zero. Two visits cite people 9 and 10,
who are not in the registry. Everything is synthetic.

```{r datos, eval = TRUE}
library(lupa)

padron <- data.frame(
  id_persona = 1:8,
  sector = rep(c("Norte", "Sur"), each = 4),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
visitas <- data.frame(
  id_visita = 1:20,
  id_persona = sprintf("%02d", c(rep(1:8, 2), 1, 2, 9, 10)),
  motivo = rep(c("control", "consulta"), length.out = 20),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
head(visitas, 3)
```

The tables are written to in-memory databases. This only prepares the example:
`lupa` does not write to the database.

```{r conexiones}
con_padron <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(con_padron, "padron", padron)
con_visitas <- suppressMessages(DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb()))
DBI::dbWriteTable(con_visitas, "visitas", visitas)
```

## Profiling each table in its engine

Each table is profiled with the connection that sees it. `perfilar_dbi()`
returns the 2 blocks of [Profiling a database](profiling-a-database.html): the
summary computed by the engine and the profile of the rows that were read.

```{r perfiles}
perfil_padron <- perfilar_dbi(con_padron, "padron")
perfil_visitas <- perfilar_dbi(con_visitas, "visitas")
```

For the cross, only one thing in the profile matters: how the key is stored.
The declared type is reported by the engine; the inferred one comes from the
rows that were read.

```{r clave-declarada}
clave_de <- function(perfil, columna) {
  fila <- perfil$perfil_muestra$columnas
  fila[
    fila$columna == columna,
    c("columna", "tipo_declarado", "tipo_inferido", "n", "n_distintos")
  ]
}
rbind(
  cbind(tabla = "padron", clave_de(perfil_padron, "id_persona")),
  cbind(tabla = "visitas", clave_de(perfil_visitas, "id_persona"))
)
```

```{r clave-declarada-cifras, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  identical(clave_de(perfil_padron, "id_persona")$tipo_declarado, "entero"),
  identical(clave_de(perfil_visitas, "id_persona")$tipo_declarado, "texto"),
  identical(clave_de(perfil_visitas, "id_persona")$tipo_inferido, "entero"),
  clave_de(perfil_padron, "id_persona")$n_distintos == nrow(padron),
  nrow(visitas) == 20L
)
```

The registry engine declares `id_persona` as an integer. The visits engine
declares it as text, although the profile, when reading it, infers an integer.
It is not a profile error: it is the first sign that the key is not stored the
same way on both sides. The visits profile records it as a finding:

```{r hallazgo}
hallazgos(perfil_visitas)[
  hallazgos(perfil_visitas)$columna == "id_persona",
  c("columna", "tipo_hallazgo", "severidad")
]
```

`tipo_declarado_distinto` does not say that a value is wrong; it says that the
text looks like a number. In the registry, the same column is an integer. That
is where the cross begins to fail. `perfilar_dbi()` does not compare the two
tables: each call sees a single connection.

## Reading only the keys

Comparing does not require the whole rows: the keys are enough. And it pays to
read them in blocks, so that the memory peak depends on the block rather than
on the size of the table. The package does not export a key reader; it is built
with `DBI::dbSendQuery()` and `DBI::dbFetch()`, the same functions with which
`perfilar_dbi()` reads from the engine.

```{r lector}
leer_por_bloques <- function(conexion, consulta, bloque = 1000) {
  resultado <- DBI::dbSendQuery(conexion, consulta)
  on.exit(DBI::dbClearResult(resultado), add = TRUE)
  partes <- list()
  repeat {
    parte <- DBI::dbFetch(resultado, n = bloque)
    if (!nrow(parte)) break
    partes[[length(partes) + 1L]] <- parte
  }
  if (length(partes)) do.call(rbind, partes) else parte
}
```

Here the block is 10 rows so that the walk is visible; in a real table, choose
the size by the available memory, not by the number of rows. The visit
identifier is read next to the key: it will later serve to locate the orphan
rows.

```{r claves}
claves_padron <- leer_por_bloques(
  con_padron, "SELECT id_persona FROM padron ORDER BY id_persona",
  bloque = 10
)
claves_visitas_crudas <- leer_por_bloques(
  con_visitas, "SELECT id_visita, id_persona FROM visitas ORDER BY id_visita",
  bloque = 10
)
data.frame(
  lado = c("padron", "visitas"),
  clase = c(
    class(claves_padron$id_persona),
    class(claves_visitas_crudas$id_persona)
  ),
  ejemplo = c(
    claves_padron$id_persona[[1]],
    claves_visitas_crudas$id_persona[[1]]
  )
)
```

```{r claves-cifras, include=FALSE}
n_padron <- nrow(claves_padron)
n_visitas <- nrow(claves_visitas_crudas)
stopifnot(
  n_padron == 8L,
  n_visitas == 20L,
  is.integer(claves_padron$id_persona),
  is.character(claves_visitas_crudas$id_persona)
)
```

The registry arrives with `r cifra(n_padron)` integer keys; the visits, with
`r cifra(n_visitas)` text keys. The first one in the registry is `1`; the first
one in the visits, `"01"`. To the eye they are the same person; for the
comparison, not yet.

## Comparing in R

`detectar_relaciones()` compares 2 data frames in memory. The first table is
the reference; the second one depends on it. `columnas_candidatas` says which
pair to compare: without it, the function tries every combination and may find
matches that are only similar codes.

```{r cruce-crudo}
cruce_crudo <- detectar_relaciones(
  claves_padron, claves_visitas_crudas,
  columnas_candidatas = list("id_persona", "id_persona")
)
cruce_crudo[, c(
  "cardinalidad", "n_valores_comunes", "cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1",
  "n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2"
)]
```

```{r cruce-crudo-cifras, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  identical(cruce_crudo$cardinalidad, "sin_coincidencias"),
  cruce_crudo$n_valores_comunes == 0,
  cruce_crudo$cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1 == 0
)
cobertura_cruda <- cruce_crudo$cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1
```

The coverage of the visits in the registry is
`r porcentaje(cobertura_cruda)`: none of the 20 visit keys matches the 8 keys
of the registry. It is not that every person is missing: it is that `"01"` and
`1` are not the same value for the comparison.

## Fixing the shape at the source

The leading zero is padding, not part of the code. It is fixed in the query,
before the value reaches R: this way the key travels with the type that will be
compared and the recipe is written in a single place. `BIGINT` is DuckDB's name
for the integer; each engine has its own.

```{r claves-corregidas}
claves_visitas <- leer_por_bloques(
  con_visitas,
  paste(
    "SELECT id_visita, CAST(id_persona AS BIGINT) AS id_persona",
    "FROM visitas ORDER BY id_visita"
  ),
  bloque = 10
)
cruce <- detectar_relaciones(
  claves_padron, claves_visitas,
  columnas_candidatas = list("id_persona", "id_persona")
)
cruce[, c(
  "cardinalidad", "n_valores_comunes", "cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1",
  "n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2"
)]
```

```{r cruce-cifras, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  identical(cruce$cardinalidad, "1:m"),
  cruce$n_valores_comunes == 8L,
  isTRUE(all.equal(cruce$cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1, 0.9)),
  identical(as.integer(cruce$n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2), 2L)
)
cobertura <- cruce$cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1
n_huerfanas <- as.integer(cruce$n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2)
n_cubiertas <- n_visitas - n_huerfanas
```

Now the coverage is `r porcentaje(cobertura)`: `r cifra(n_cubiertas)` of the
`r cifra(n_visitas)` visits find their person. There remain
`r cifra(n_huerfanas)` orphan visits, the ones of people 9 and 10, who are not
in the registry.

```{r huerfanas}
huerfanas <- cruce$huerfanas_tabla2[[1]]
data.frame(
  total = huerfanas$total,
  mostradas = huerfanas$mostrados,
  estado = huerfanas$estado,
  alcance = huerfanas$alcance
)
claves_visitas$id_visita[huerfanas$indices_fila]
```

The trace does not publish the key values; it publishes the row positions. With
`id_visita` read next to the key, those positions translate to visits 19 and
20. In a large table, the read order has to be stable for the position to keep
working: that is why the query carries `ORDER BY`.

## From the comparison to the metric

A loose coverage is useful for this delivery. Comparing deliveries requires a
measure with a name, a date and an identifier. `ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad`
measures the proportion of non-missing keys of the second entity that exist in
the first one.

```{r metrica}
nucleo <- metricas_nucleo()
regla <- instanciar(
  especializar(
    nucleo$ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad,
    nombre_especifico = "VisitaTienePersona"
  ),
  entidad = c("padron", "visitas"),
  atributos = c("id_persona", "id_persona")
)
medicion <- medir(
  modelo(regla),
  list(padron = claves_padron, visitas = claves_visitas),
  id_medicion = "cruce-2026-01",
  fecha = "2026-01-31"
)
medicion[, c("metrica_especifica", "objeto_medible", "resultado")]
```

```{r metrica-cifras, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  nrow(medicion) == 1L,
  isTRUE(all.equal(medicion$resultado, cobertura)),
  identical(medicion$entidad, "visitas"),
  identical(medicion$atributo, "id_persona")
)
```

The metric returns a single row: the coverage of the foreign key, with the rule
name, the dependent entity and the object measured. The `id_medicion` and the
`fecha` are what make it possible to compare this run with the next one. An
`NA` in the foreign key does not count as an orphan: it is not a value that was
looked up, so it does not enter the denominator.

The metric does not normalize anything. If it is passed the raw keys, it
measures `r porcentaje(cobertura_cruda)`, which is the correct figure for that
shape. The correction is made earlier, in the query, and applied to both sides.

## When the keys do not have the same shape {#cuando-las-claves-no-tienen-la-misma-forma}

The visits case was a leading zero. There are 2 more that show up often:
uppercase and edge spaces. The in-memory comparison ignores neither.

```{r formas}
codigos_a <- data.frame(codigo = c("A-01", "B-02", " C-03"))
codigos_b <- data.frame(codigo = c("a-01", "b-02", "c-03"))
comparar <- function(a, b) {
  detectar_relaciones(
    a, b, columnas_candidatas = list("codigo", "codigo")
  )$n_valores_comunes
}
c(
  crudo = comparar(codigos_a, codigos_b),
  normalizado = comparar(
    data.frame(codigo = toupper(trimws(codigos_a$codigo))),
    data.frame(codigo = toupper(trimws(codigos_b$codigo)))
  )
)
```

```{r formas-cifras, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  comparar(codigos_a, codigos_b) == 0,
  comparar(
    data.frame(codigo = toupper(trimws(codigos_a$codigo))),
    data.frame(codigo = toupper(trimws(codigos_b$codigo)))
  ) == 3
)
```

Text versus number is not a problem of classes, but of spelling. An integer and
a double with the same integer value match, and a text `"1"` matches the number
`1`; but `"01"`, `"1.0"` or `" 1"` do not. The comparison uses the exact
identity of the value: it neither trims spaces nor changes case. The same
happens with dates: `"2026-01-31"` matches a `Date`, but `"31/01/2026"` does
not.

The decision of which shape is canonical belongs to the data, not to the
package. If the leading zero is padding, remove it on read; if it is part of
the code, restore it on both sides. If case does not distinguish, normalize
both tables with the same function; if it does, normalizing would be an error.
And if the spaces are accidental, trim them on both sides. What you cannot do
is fix only one side and call the result coverage.

## What the package does not do {#lo-que-el-paquete-no-hace}

It does not join two connections in a single query. `perfilar_dbi()`,
`medir_dbi()`, `perfilar_coleccion()` and `relaciones_coleccion()` receive one
connection or one collection; `detectar_relaciones()` and `medir()` compare
data frames in R. That is the boundary: each engine profiles and projects its
own side, and R brings the keys together.

If the two tables were in the same database, `medir_dbi()` could resolve the
rule in the engine, through the `sql_dedicado_referencial` path. With two
connections there is no query that sees both, and that is why the recipe brings
the keys over. That bounded read also protects the data: the full rows do not
travel, only the identifiers needed for the comparison.

Neither does it normalize for you: the comparison is exact. And it does not
decide whether a relationship is a real foreign key. Coverage is evidence; the
data dictionary and the engine constraints are what confirm it. Coverage is
computed over every key it is given: there is no implicit sample that could
align with the data. If a subset is read, the coverage is of that subset and
that has to be said.

The two reads are from different moments. If the databases change between them,
the coverage mixes two snapshots: it pays to read the keys as close together as
possible and record the run date, as is done with the metric.

## Summary

- `perfilar_dbi()` describes each table in its engine. The declared type of the
  key and the `tipo_declarado_distinto` finding warn when the two sides are not
  written the same way.
- Reading only the keys and in blocks bounds the memory peak: `dbSendQuery()` +
  `dbFetch(n)` walk the table without bringing the full rows.
- `detectar_relaciones()` measures coverage in the 2 directions and names the
  orphan rows; `medir()` with `ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad` turns it into a
  measure with a date and an identifier.
- The comparison is exact: leading zeros, uppercase and spaces are distinct
  values. Normalizing both sides with the same rule, or fixing the type in the
  query, is part of the recipe.
- The package does not cross two connections in a single query: each database
  is read separately and R is the meeting point.
